# Research Agenda

My research examines human-AI work allocation and decision authority in service operations. I study how AI, GenAI, and AI agents reshape work in service systems and digital platforms, with a focus on human-AI collaboration and service performance.

The agenda is empirical and field-grounded. I use field experiments, platform data, causal inference, machine learning, and LLM-based text analysis to study how firms should design, evaluate, and govern AI-enabled operations.

::: {.content-band .philosophy-band}
## Research Philosophy

::: {.philosophy-note}
I take inspiration from von Neumann's view that formal disciplines stay vital when they repeatedly return to their empirical sources. Models, methods, and metrics are most useful when they are replenished by ideas drawn from reality.

朱熹说：“问渠哪得清如许，为有源头活水来。” 对我而言，这句诗表达了同样的研究观：学术问题的清澈与生命力，来自对现实问题和未来发展的持续思考。
:::

This perspective shapes how I study AI-enabled operations. AI changes operations not only by automating tasks, but also by changing who observes problems, who intervenes, who bears responsibility for service failures, and how platforms allocate scarce human attention. My research begins from this operational view of AI systems.

Rather than treating AI performance as a standalone technical outcome, I study how AI interacts with process design, worker behavior, customer experience, and platform governance. This is especially important in service operations, where outcomes often depend on both visible customer-facing interaction and less visible resolution work.

My goal is to develop evidence that is useful for both academic theory and managerial decision-making: when AI agents should act autonomously, when humans should intervene, how organizations should measure service performance, and how platforms can design more reliable human-AI operating systems.
:::

## Research Streams

::: {.stream-grid}
::: {.stream-card}
### GenAI and Service Operations

I study how GenAI changes service processes, including customer service speed, quality, escalation, and recovery, using customer-service operations as an empirical setting.
:::

::: {.stream-card}
### AI Agents and Platform Operations

I examine how agentic AI systems operate inside platform-mediated service environments, including Alibaba Taobao customer service operations.
:::

::: {.stream-card}
### Human-AI Collaboration in Operational Systems

I study human-in-the-loop intervention, AI failure recovery, intervention timing, and worker effort in hybrid service systems where AI and human workers share responsibility for outcomes.
:::
:::
:::

## Working Papers

<div class="paper-meta">(Job Market paper, *co-first authorship), major revision at <em>Operations Research</em></div>

### Agentic AI and Human-in-the-Loop Interventions: Field Experimental Evidence from Alibaba's Customer Service Operations

Yiwei Wang\*, **Chuan Zhu**\*, Tianjun Feng, Lauren Xiaoyuan Lu, and Bingxin Jia.

- **Third Prize, 2026 INFORMS Service Science Best Student Paper Competition.**
- **Best Paper Nominee, CIST 2026.**

This paper uses a randomized field experiment involving 647 workers and approximately 681,000 customer-service chats at Alibaba Taobao. It finds that agentic AI reduces average chat duration but may lower customer ratings. Descriptive post-escalation analyses show more favorable outcomes after technical than emotional escalations, with differences in intervention timing and human effort.

**Methods and setting:** randomized field experiment; causal inference using large-scale customer service operational data; LLM annotation; Alibaba Taobao customer service operations.

::: {.paper-entry}
<div class="paper-meta">Working paper</div>

### Talk the Talk and Walk the Walk: An Empirical Study of Front-Office Communication and Back-Office Problem Solving Under Workload Pressure

**Chuan Zhu**, Tom Fangyun Tan, and Tianjun Feng.

This paper examines how workload changes agents' within-session allocation between front-office communication and back-office problem solving at a large Chinese e-commerce platform. The analyzed sample contains 3,965,028 sessions handled by 7,004 agents. Workload has a U-shaped relationship with the share of effort devoted to communication, and this allocation helps explain service speed, customer ratings, and retrials. Textual analyses distinguish the benefits of effective interaction from the crowding out of substantive problem solving. Counterfactual estimates suggest that rebalancing effort can improve all three outcomes without additional capacity.

**Methods and setting:** service records, clickstream data, and chat transcripts; instrumental-variable control-function estimation; nonlinear mediation and counterfactual analysis; LDA-based problem-centeredness and LLM-based interaction-quality measures; after-sales live-chat customer service.

:::

## Selected Projects

::: {.paper-list}
::: {.paper-entry}
### Agentic AI in Customer Service Operations

This project studies AI-agent deployment with human-in-the-loop supervision in Alibaba Taobao's customer service operations. It connects to the GenAI and Service Operations, AI Agents and Platform Operations, and Human-AI Collaboration streams.
:::

::: {.paper-entry}
### Workload and Effort Allocation in Online Service

This project studies how service workload affects the allocation of visible customer-facing interaction and less visible resolution work in live-chat customer service operations. It connects to service operations, platform operations, and empirical methods for AI-enabled operations.
:::
